summary: Describes how an IPv6 host with several prefixes from different upstream networks should pick its first-hop router. Networks may filter packets by source address, so sending through the wrong router can get traffic dropped.

plainLanguage.summary: If you have two mail carriers who each only accept letters with certain return addresses, you must give each letter to the right one. This explains how a computer should choose.

questions: ipv6 host with multiple prefixes router selection
which router should a multihomed ipv6 host use
how does an ipv6 host choose a first hop router
why do multihomed hosts need source based router selection
subtitle: How a host with several provider prefixes should pick the first-hop router that matches its source address.

tldr.problem: A host with addresses from several upstream networks may send a packet to the wrong router, and BCP 38 ingress filters or stateful firewalls can then discard it.
tldr.mechanism: The host remembers which prefixes each router advertised in its Prefix Information Options and prefers a router that advertised the packet's source prefix, whatever the Default Router Preference.
tldr.outcome: Packets reach an exit that will accept them, with no routing protocol needed between the routers. The RFC updates RFC 4861 to extend host and router behavior.

today: RFC 8028 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4861, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Multi-Prefix Problem
sections.content:
The RFC describes IPv6 host behavior in a network with more than one prefix, each allocated by an upstream network assumed to apply BCP 38 ingress filtering (RFC 2827), where the host can choose among several routers. A packet sent to the wrong egress is liable to be discarded by the filter.

The same trouble arises with stateful firewalls, where return packets are dropped if they do not come back through the firewall that created the state, and with unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF). The RFC uses "filter" for all of these. A host cannot know which kind of filter is in place, so it says the only known consistent solution is to implement the features it defines.
sections.plainLanguage: Some doors only let in people wearing the right badge. If you walk up to the wrong door with your badge, you get turned away.

sections.title: What the Host Expects of the Network
sections.content:
A host learns its prefixes from Router Advertisements (RAs), and forms addresses with SLAAC or DHCPv6. The simple cases are a LAN with one router per upstream network (a multihomed network), or a host served by disjoint networks on separate interfaces (a multihomed host). With no routing protocol among the routers, packets cannot be reliably forwarded between them to dodge filters, and an indirect route would be inefficient anyway. So the host should pick the right router itself.

In such networks each prefix SHOULD be advertised in a Prefix Information Option (PIO) by one of the attached routers, even if addresses come from DHCPv6. A router advertising a prefix signals that it can route packets with source addresses in that prefix, regardless of the L and A flags. A PIO with both flags cleared SHOULD be sent where appropriate, and a host SHOULD NOT ignore it. The RFC also expects networking equipment to support source/destination routing for at least some routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router puts up a sign saying which return addresses it handles. Computers should read the signs, even plain ones.

sections.title: Router Selection by the Host
sections.content:
The core change is to how the host reads Router Advertisements. The host's record of each default router SHOULD include the prefixes it announced. A PIO is reinterpreted to also mean that the advertising router is a reasonable first hop for any packet whose source address is in that prefix, regardless of Default Router Preference.

For default router selection (extending Section 6.3.6 of RFC 4861), a host SHOULD select default routers for each prefix it holds an address in. Routers that advertised the prefix SHOULD be preferred over those that did not. Among several routers advertising the same prefix, the host chooses using the criteria of RFC 4191. If no router advertised the prefix, normal routing metrics apply, as with a host that also has a VPN.

When replying, the source address is forced to be the address the peer used. That fixes which router the reply must use. When starting a conversation, a Route Information Option on one router may reasonably influence which source address the host picks.
sections.plainLanguage: When sending a letter, look at your return address first, then hand it to the carrier whose sign lists that address.

sections.title: Source Addresses, Redirects and History
sections.content:
The approach depends on Rule 5.5 of RFC 6724: choose a source address from a prefix advertised by the next-hop router for the destination. A host following the router selection rules SHOULD implement this rule.

Hosts SHOULD apply off-link redirects only to the specific pair of source and destination addresses concerned, so the Destination Cache may need source-specific entries. Hosts that keep history of what worked SHOULD record the prefix after a successful exchange, whatever the L and A flags were, and MAY reuse an address in that prefix with the same destination later.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer remembers which carrier delivered each letter successfully, and uses the same one next time. If a helper says "try another carrier", it only applies to that one return address and destination.

sections.title: Host Models and Residual Issues
sections.content:
The RFC compares its approach to the strong and weak host models in RFC 1122. It is most similar to the strong host model, since both route on source and destination. The difference is that it picks a router, not an interface, so a multi-interface router with a common prefix across several LANs may be reached over either LAN.

Residual issues remain. If all routers on a link advertise all prefixes, a packet may take one extra hop through the wrong router. In the disjoint LAN case, the wrong router cannot find or route to the right one, so the host must memorize and select the best first hop itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a letter goes to the wrong carrier who passes it on, costing a bit of time. If the carriers cannot talk to each other, you have to choose the right one yourself.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC aims to avoid connectivity problems with BCP 38 filters or stateful firewalls combined with multihoming, and it does not create new security or privacy exposures in itself. Because routing now works where it failed before, networks that were unreachable might become unexpectedly exposed.

There may be a small privacy gain. Today a multihomed host that sends packets with the wrong address to an upstream discloses the prefix of one upstream to the other, and this practice reduces that. The RFC makes no IANA requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixing the delivery mix-up can open doors that used to be stuck shut. It also means you tell each carrier less about your other carrier.
